Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette:
Elena Wagner is a 26-year-old firefighter who had been proud of the steadiness she brought to chaotic scenes before she was taken captive during a call nearly a year ago. Her engine company had responded to a warehouse fire where, amid the confusion, she was separated from the rest of the crew and trapped by two men who had been inside the building. They locked her in a cramped storage room while smoke seeped under the door and shouted at her each time she pounded to get out. She remembers the crush of bodies in the hallway just before she was forced inside, the dim light, and a wall pinned with old Polaroids of workers and family members curling at the edges. What stays with her most is how sharply each image remains: the streak of soot on the door handle, the angle of a boot near her face, the photographs on the wall. When she speaks about it now, she says the scenes come back not like remembering but like looking at photographs in her mind, too vivid and too immediate to feel like ordinary memory.

In the weeks after she was freed, Elena found that specific moments in daily life could pull those images forward without warning. At the firehouse, someone showing around old station pictures or a framed retirement photo on the wall could abruptly bring the storage room back with unnerving clarity. On grocery runs after shift, crowded aisles and people pressing too close made her feel flooded and disoriented, and a memory of the event would come into her mind all at once, as if it had been waiting just beneath the surface. Those same moments did more than remind her. Seeing old photos or getting hemmed in by a crowd would be followed by a sickening thought that there was something fundamentally altered in her now, that she was no longer the capable woman who had once run toward danger. Once she had begun reading herself as damaged and unable to cope, she moved through the station and the city as if ordinary details might expose that fragility; framed pictures, narrow aisles, and people standing too close snagged her attention precisely because she no longer trusted herself to handle what they might stir up. She had come to believe that the way she acted in those minutes of captivity-her fear, her hesitation, her failure to get herself out-meant the event happened because of something weak in her.

That conclusion has gradually become the lens through which she understands herself. Elena says she does not know who she is anymore, and she is certain she cannot handle even minor upset. Because she sees herself as diminished and responsible, any sign of internal strain feels like proof that she is unraveling, and she stays braced for the next surge of panic. Even in her apartment with the doors locked, she cannot relax. Ordinary sounds-a dropped pan in the kitchen downstairs, the station alarm during a quiet shift, a radio crackling unexpectedly-make her jump hard enough to spill what she is holding. Living with that level of alarm became, for Elena, its own kind of proof that she had been fundamentally changed. The fact that she felt under threat so often and so quickly hardened her belief that she was no longer steady, no longer safe in herself, and not the firefighter she had been. When that happens, she is quickly back inside the event, suddenly feeling as if she is there again rather than here in the present. Her sense that she is no longer able to cope also shapes the way the memories return: she describes them as belonging to someone else and yet being more real than the room she is sitting in, as though her mind cannot place them in the past or fully claim them as hers.

The memories themselves deepen the damage to how she sees herself. Because they arrive as frozen, photographic fragments with such force, Elena takes their vividness as evidence that the captivity has permanently marked her. After one of these jolting images, she would spend hours keyed up and searching her surroundings for anything that matched it, noticing walls covered in photos, blocked doorways, and pockets of crowding she might otherwise have overlooked. The memory did not end when the image faded; it trained her attention onto reminders of itself. After a flash of the storage room door or the old photos on the wall, she is left thinking, no one who was still normal would remember things like this. The more alien the memory feels, the more she doubts her own identity; the more real it feels, the more she blames herself for not having acted differently. She has also become increasingly preoccupied with the kinds of situations that might set the memory off. Before entering a crowded bar with colleagues, she scans the room for exits and for walls covered in pictures. Walking through the station, she notices framed photos immediately. Her mind seems to sort the world by what might bring it all back.

That constant readiness keeps the cycle going. When she startles or has a flashback, she becomes even more watchful for crowds, old photos, and any hint that a sudden memory might be coming. After rough shifts she avoids the day room if too many people are gathered there, and she takes the long way around the hallway with the department's historical photo display. Those choices have begun to cost her. She eats alone more often at work, and a captain recently commented that she seems absent from the camaraderie that used to come naturally to her. Yet the vigilance feels necessary to Elena, because each jolt of fear convinces her again that she is fragile, changed, and unable to manage what might happen if she lets her guard down. By the time she sought help, she was frightened not only of the memories but of what they seemed to say about her-that the decisive firefighter she had been is gone for good. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is that she might find some way to feel like the memories are hers and in the past, rather than something that can overtake her at any moment.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show Elena’s negative appraisals causing her to notice, generate, or become more sensitive to triggers within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly convey that Elena’s intrusive memories lead her to identify or become more focused on triggers/reminders in a causal way within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not clearly state that Elena’s sense of threat directly produces or intensifies her negative appraisals within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show Elena’s negative appraisals causing her to notice, generate, or become more sensitive to triggers within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey that Elena’s intrusive memories lead her to identify or become more focused on triggers/reminders in a causal way within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that Elena’s sense of threat directly produces or intensifies her negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
